Rather, it appears that since the entire biblical passage is framed in the direct second person ("and you shall love"), the Torah should grammatically have written merely b'lekhet ("in walking");
רַק לְכָךְ שִׁנָּה תֵּבַת "בַּדֶּרֶךְ", וְלֹא "בְּדַרְכְּךָ" כְּמוֹ "בְּבֵיתֶךָ", לְאוֹרוֹיֵי דְּכֻלְּהוּ לְדִיּוּקָא, וְזֶהוּ "כִּי דֶּרֶךְ"

and the reason Scripture varied the phrase to say "in the way" (baderekh) instead of "in your way" (b'darkecha), parallel to "in your house" (b'veitecha), was to teach that both phrases yield precise halachic exclusions, which is the meaning of "just as 'way' is optional."
שָׁם [עַמּוּד ב׳]: "אֵין קוֹרִין 'אָבוֹת' אֶלָּא לִשְׁלֹשָׁה" וְכוּלֵי
There (Berakhot 16b): "We do not call any 'Patriarchs' (avot) except three [Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob], nor 'Matriarchs' (imahot) except four":
פֵּרוּשׁ: הַתֹּאַר "אָב" בַּמֶּה שֶׁהוּא זוֹכֶה לִבְנוֹ בַּחֲמִשָּׁה דְּבָרִים (עֵדֻיּוֹת פֶּרֶק ב׳ מִשְׁנָה ט׳), וְהַבֵּן נִמְשָׁךְ מִכֹּחוֹ
The definition of the title "Father" consists of his transmitting spiritual merit to his son in five matters (Eduyot 2:9), the son deriving directly from his essential spiritual vitality
[דִּבְלָאו הָכֵי גַּם שׁוֹר גַּם שֶׂה יֵשׁ לָהֶם אָבוֹת, אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵין לָאָב שַׁיָּכוּת בְּכֹחַ הַבֵּן
[for otherwise, an ox or a lamb also has male progenitors, yet the animal sire possesses no spiritual bearing on its offspring.
וּבָזֶה יֵשׁ לוֹמַר מַה שֶּׁנֶּעֱנַשׁ שֵׁם דְּלֹא זָכָה לִכְהֻנָּה מֵחֲלָצָיו (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב נְדָרִים דַּף ל״ב עַמּוּד ב׳)
Through this we can understand why Shem was penalized such that the priesthood did not issue from his loins (Nedarim 32b):
וְקָשֶׁה: הָא אַבְרָהָם גַּם כֵּן לֹא כָּל בָּנָיו הָיוּ כֹּהֲנִים, וְגַם לֹא תֵּכֶף, רַק אַחַר כַּמָּה דּוֹרוֹת זָכָה אַהֲרֹן לִכְהֻנָּה
now this is difficult, for not all of Abraham's sons were priests either, and Aaron merited the priesthood only generations later;
וַהֲרֵי הוּא כָּךְ מִיּוֹצְאֵי חַלְצֵי שֵׁם כְּמוֹ מִיּוֹצְאֵי חַלְצֵי אַבְרָהָם, וּמַה נָפְקָא מִנַּהּ דְּשֵׁם לֹא זָכָה וְאַבְרָהָם זָכָה?
and Aaron was just as much a descendant of Shem as he was of Abraham, so what difference does it make that Shem did not merit it while Abraham did?
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּשֵׁם לֹא זָכָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מִכֹּחוֹ וְיִהְיֶה הוּא הָאָב שֶׁמִּתְּחִלָּה הָיָה מוּכָן לִזְכּוֹת הַכְּהֻנָּה מִכֹּחוֹ, וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִלְקַח
One must answer: Shem did not merit that the priesthood should flow from his spiritual agency as its founding Father, for that pristine potential was stripped from him;
וְרַק אַבְרָהָם נִקְרָא "אָב", וְאֵין קוֹרִין "אָבוֹת" אֶלָּא לִשְׁלֹשָׁה
and Abraham alone was crowned "Father," for we designate as Patriarchs only three;
אֲבָל שֵׁם, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא מִיּוֹצְאֵי חֲלָצָיו, אֵין נִקְרָא "אָב" וְאֵין נִקְרָא מִזַּרְעוֹ
whereas Shem, though an ancestor, is not designated the "Father" of the covenant nor are they identified as his covenantal seed.

וְהִנֵּה אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם תְּחִלָּה לַגֵּרִים (סֻכָּה דַּף מ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳), וְגֵר כְּקָטָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד וְאֵין לוֹ יִחוּס אָבוֹת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בָּבָא קַמָּא דַּף פ״ח עַמּוּד א׳)
Moreover, Abraham was the first of converts (Sukkah 49b), and a convert is like a newborn child without legal paternity (Bava Kamma 88a);
לְכָךְ אֵין קוֹרִין וְכוּלֵי רַק מֵאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ וְאֵילָךְ]
therefore covenantal fatherhood begins strictly from Abraham onward].
וְהָאֵם, לְפִי שֶׁמְּשֻׁעְבֶּדֶת וְאֵין לָהּ כֹּחַ בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָהּ, אֵין הִיא הַזּוֹכָה
And the Mother, being bound in marriage and lacking independent patriarchal authority, is not the primary conveyor of covenantal status;
רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם לְמַה שֶּׁגַּם הוּא מְשֻׁעְבָד לָהּ לְמַלֹּאות חֶסְרוֹנָהּ, נִמְצָא יֵשׁ לָהּ כֹּחַ זֶה שֶׁל מִלּוּי הַחִסָּרוֹן
nevertheless, because the husband is obligated to fulfill her marital and emotional needs, she possesses the power of filling human void and deficiency.
וְזֶה הוֹרָאַת תֹּאַר "אֵם", שֶׁהִיא הַמּוֹלִידָתוֹ וְעוֹשָׂה מֵאַיִן וְחָסֵר יֵשׁ וּמִלּוּי
And this is the essential meaning of "Mother": she gives birth, transforming nothingness and lack into existence and completion;
וְזֶהוּ בְּכֹחָהּ, שֶׁאֵלָיו תְּשׁוּקָתָהּ לְמִלּוּי חֶסְרוֹנָהּ
and this rests in her power, her deepest yearning being the fulfillment of deficiency.
וְזֶהוּ: "וּבֵן כְּסִיל — תּוּגַת אִמּוֹ", שֶׁהוּא בַּעַל חֶסְרוֹנוֹת
Thus Scripture states: "A foolish son is the grief of his mother," for he remains full of deficiencies;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן "בֵּן חָכָם" — בַּעַל מַעֲלָה לְבַד מִלּוּי חֶסְרוֹן — "יְשַׂמַּח אָב", שֶׁמִּכֹּחוֹ הוּא
whereas "a wise son"—possessing spiritual excellence far beyond mere filling of deficiency—"makes a glad father," for that positive vitality stems directly from him.
וּלְכָךְ אָמְרוּ (בִּיבָמוֹת דַּף ס״ב עַמּוּד א׳, וּבְבָבָא קַמָּא דַּף ט״ו עַמּוּד א׳ וְדַף פ״ח עַמּוּד א׳) דְּעֶבֶד אֵין לוֹ יִחוּס
Therefore the Sages stated (Yevamot 62a; Bava Kamma 15a, 88a) that a Canaanite slave possesses no legal lineage,
וּבַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דִּיבָמוֹת וְקִדּוּשִׁין: כְּפַר בֶּן בָּקָר
and in the Jerusalem Talmud: he is legally likened to a calf;
דְּעֶבֶד אֵין לוֹ שׁוּם כֹּחַ בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ [אֲפִילּוּ כֹּחַ הַטּוֹב בְּיַד הָרַב לְשַׁחְרְרוֹ וּלְחַיְּבוֹ בְּמִצְוֹת]
for a slave has no legal standing of his own [even the capacity for holiness remains in the master's hand to emancipate him and obligate him in mitzvot],
רַק הַכֹּל קָנוּי לְרַבּוֹ, וּמֵאַיִן יִהְיֶה לוֹ כֹּחַ לְהַנְחִיל לַבֵּן
but everything belongs to his owner, so whence could he derive the power to bequeath covenantal lineage to a son?
[וּכְעֵין שֶׁאִיתָא בְּקִדּוּשִׁין (דַּף ל׳ עַמּוּד ב׳): אִשָּׁה לֹא נֶאֱמַר "כַּבֵּד", שֶׁרְשׁוּת [אֲחֵרִים עָלֶיהָ] וְכוּלֵי, וְאֵין יְכוֹלָה לְכַבֵּד לְזוּלָתָהּ]

[Similar to what is taught in Kiddushin (30b): concerning a married woman Scripture does not mandate honoring parents equally, for the authority of her husband is upon her, leaving her unable to dedicate herself fully to others].
וְהִנֵּה אִיתָא (בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה נ״ד): "עַד כָּאן רַחֲמֵי הָאָב" וְכוּלֵי
Behold, it is taught in Bereishit Rabbah (parashah 54): "Thus far reach the paternal mercies of the father," etc.,
שֶׁאֵין זוֹכֶה רַק עַד דּוֹר שְׁלִישִׁי, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב: "וַעֲטֶרֶת זְקֵנִים בְּנֵי בָנִים"
teaching that a biological father conveys merit only up to the third generation (grandchildren), as written: "Children's children are the crown of the aged"
[אֲבָל "תִּפְאֶרֶת בָּנִים" רַק "אֲבוֹתָם", וְלֹא דּוֹר ג׳ לְמַעְלָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר]
[whereas "the glory of children" is strictly "their fathers," but not three generations ascending upward to a great-grandfather, as I wrote elsewhere],
וְלֹא יוֹתֵר, דְּאֵין כֹּחוֹ חָזָק כָּל כָּךְ לִהְיוֹת מַשֶּׁהוּ שֶׁבְּתַעֲרוֹבֵי תַּעֲרוֹבֵי תַּעֲרוֹבוֹת מוֹעִיל לְפַעְפֵּעַ בְּכֻלּוֹ
and no further, for an ordinary ancestor's personal spiritual power is not strong enough for a minute trace to diffuse and permeate through an unbroken chain of multiple mixtures.
וְהִנֵּה בְּדָבָר חָשׁוּב קַיְימָא לָן דְּהַתַּעֲרוֹבוֹת הַשְּׁלִישִׁי מוּתָּר (עַיֵּן בֵּיצָה דַּף ג׳ עַמּוּד ב׳ וּשְׁאָר דּוּכְתֵי)

Now, even regarding a halachically significant object (davar chashuv that normally cannot be nullified), the established rule is that a tertiary mixture is permitted (see Beitzah 3b and other places);
אֲבָל אֵלּוּ אֲבָהָן דְּעָלְמָא הָיָה כֹּחָם חָזָק לְפַעְפֵּעַ עַד סוֹף כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת
but these universal Patriarchs of the world (Avahan D'Alma) possessed spiritual potency so immense that it diffuses throughout the end of all generations,
מוּשְׁרָשׁ בְּטֶבַע כָּל אִישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל מִטִּבְעָם, כַּנּוֹדָע, וּלְכָךְ: "אֵין קוֹרִין" וְכוּלֵי
ingrained as the second nature of every Jew from their very essence, as is known; therefore the Gemara establishes: "We do not call any 'Patriarchs' [except three]."
[וְהַתֹּאַר "אַבָּא" פֵּרוּשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁקּוֹרִין עַכְשָׁו לְיָשִׁישׁ: "זְקֵנִי", וְזֶה לֹא שַׁיָּךְ בַּעֲבָדִים שֶׁאֵינָם אָבוֹת אַף לִבְנֵיהֶם

[And the honorific title Abba (Father) is used respectfully as one currently addresses an elder as "my grandfather," which cannot apply to Canaanite slaves who lack legal paternity even toward their own biological children;
וְלָכֵן נֶאֱמַר כָּבוֹד [וְאַהֲבָה] בְּאֵם, וּמוֹרָא בְּאָב
and therefore honor [and love] is biblically emphasized regarding the Mother, while reverent awe is emphasized regarding the Father:
כִּי הָאַהֲבָה לְמִי שֶׁמַּשְׁלִים חֶסְרוֹנוֹ, כְּעִנְיַן "וְאֵלַיִךְ תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ"
for love flows naturally toward one who nurtures and fills one's deficiency, in the sense of "and unto you shall be his longing";
וְיִרְאָה לְהַשְׁלִים הַמַּעֲלָה, כְּתַלְמִיד לְרַב וְעֶבֶד לְאָדוֹן
while reverent awe is directed toward emulating superior spiritual excellence, like a student toward a master or a servant toward a sovereign
[וּלְכָךְ יִרְאָה נֶגֶד הַלֹּא תַעֲשֶׂה, וְאַהֲבָה נֶגֶד עֲשֵׂה, שֶׁעַל כֵּן צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת שָׁלֵם בְּצַד ב׳, וְדַיֵּק]
[and therefore Awe corresponds to negative prohibitions, while Love corresponds to positive commandments, necessitating wholeness on both sides; examine this closely]].
וּבְנֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם: הַמֹּחַ — "אָב" בְּחָכְמָתוֹ לִכְלֵי הַמַּעֲשִׂים
Within the human soul: the brain functions as the "Father" through its wisdom (Chochmah), directing the active limbs of deed;
וְהַלֵּב — "אֵם" בְּבִינָתָהּ לְהַשְׁלָמַת הַחִסָּרוֹן, כַּנּוֹדָע בַּזֹּהַר
while the heart serves as the "Mother" through its understanding (Binah), nurturing and rectifying deficiency, as known from the Zohar.
וְזֶהוּ קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע וּתְפִלָּה: קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע — קַבָּלַת עוֹל מַלְכוּת שָׁמַיִם וּמִצְוֹת, שְׁלֵמוּת מַעֲלָתוֹ

And this embodies the dichotomy between the Shema and the Amidah prayer: the Shema is the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven and the commandments, representing the transcendent perfection of man's spiritual stature;
וּתְפִלָּה — לְמַלֹּאות חֶסְרוֹנוֹ, וְהוּא אַחַר כַּוָּנַת הַלֵּב
while prayer is crying out to fill one's deficiencies, depending fundamentally upon the inward devotion of the heart.
וְזֶהוּ: "אֲבָרֶכְךָ בְחַיָּי" — זֶה קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע (בְּרָכוֹת שָׁם), מִצַּד מַעֲלַת עַצְמוֹ
And this is the verse: "'I will bless You while I live'—this refers to the Shema" (Berakhot 16b), representing the intrinsic spiritual elevation of one's living essence;
"וּבְשִׁמְךָ [אֶשָּׂא כַפָּי]" — זֶה תְּפִלָּה, שֶׁהוּא חָסֵר מִכְּלוּם, רַק בְּשִׁמְךָ, מִצִּדְּךָ, שֶׁתְּמַלֵּא חֶסְרוֹנוֹ

"'and in Your Name [I will lift up my hands]'—this refers to Prayer," where man stands utterly empty and deficient of everything, pleading solely by virtue of Your Name and grace to replenish his lack.
וּלְכָךְ תְּפִלָּה אַחַר קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע, שֶׁאַחַר כָּל הַשְּׁלֵמוּת יַכִּיר כִּי הוּא חָסֵר, וְאָז כְּמוֹ וְכוּלֵי, שֶׁתַּכְלִית הַיְדִיעָה שֶׁלֹּא נֵדַע

Therefore prayer must follow the Shema: only after realizing the highest summit of perfection does man recognize that he remains fundamentally destitute before God, wherein the ultimate apex of knowledge is to know that we do not know.
וְזֶהוּ: "תִּשְׂבַּע נַפְשִׁי", תַּכְלִית הַשְּׂבִיעָה בַּתַּאֲווֹת [גַּם בְּרוּחָנִיּוּת כֵּן, וְדַיֵּק]: "כְּשֶׁמַּרְעִיבוֹ — שָׂבֵעַ" (סֻכָּה דַּף נ״ב עַמּוּד א׳)

And this is "my soul shall be sated": the ultimate satiety of spiritual desire [operating equally in the spiritual realm; examine this] follows the paradox of the inclination: "when one starves it, it is sated" (Sukkah 52a).
וְהֵם שְׁנֵי עוֹלָמוֹת: הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה — תַּשְׁלוּם הַחִסָּרוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (אָבוֹת פֶּרֶק ד׳ מִשְׁנָה כ״ב): "יָפָה שָׁעָה אַחַת" וְכוּלֵי

These correspond to the two cosmic realms: this present world is the arena for rectifying deficiency, as taught in Pirkei Avot (4:22): "Better is one hour [of repentance and good deeds in this world than all the life of the World to Come],"
כִּי יוֹתֵר שָׂמֵחַ הֶעָנִי כְּשֶׁמַּעֲשִׁיר מֵעָשִׁיר שֶׁמַּעֲשִׁיר יוֹתֵר
for an impoverished pauper who becomes wealthy experiences far greater joy than a rich man who merely increases his riches.
וְזֶהוּ מִדַּת לַיְלָה, שֶׁאָז דַּי תַּשְׁלוּם הַחִסָּרוֹן [כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל גַּם כֵּן] שֶׁל הַנִּיתּוּךְ עַל יְדֵי הַשֵּׁנָה
And this is the quality of the night, wherein replenishing the deficit [as noted above] caused by bodily dissolution during sleep is sufficient;
וְזֶהוּ "אֵין רִנָּה שֶׁל תּוֹרָה" וְכוּלֵי (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה פֶּרֶק מ״ז), שֶׁהוּא תַּבְלִין לְיֵצֶר הָרָע
and this explains "the song of Torah is found only at night" (Shemot Rabbah 47), serving as the curative spice against the evil inclination.
וְזֶהוּ "וֶאֱמוּנָתְךָ" — הַקִּוּוּי, וְאֵין מְקַוֶּה אֶלָּא מִי שֶׁחָסֵר, זֶה בַּלֵּילוֹת
And this is "and Your faithfulness (emunah)"—which connotes yearning and hope, for only one who lacks can truly hope, and this belongs to the nights;
וְהָעוֹלָם הַבָּא — שְׁלֵמוּת מַעֲלוֹת, דּוֹמֶה לְיוֹם, שֶׁהוּא זְמַן הַפְּעֻלָּה
whereas the World to Come represents the transcendent fullness of spiritual attainments, likened to the day, which is the time of radiant activity.
שָׁם (בְּרָכוֹת דַּף ט״ז עַמּוּד ב׳): "אַחֲרִית וְתִקְוָה"
There in the Gemara (Berakhot 16b): Rabbi Chiya prayed: "grant us a future (acharit) and hope (tikvah)":
פֵּרוּשׁ: לְכָל מַדְרֵגָה יֵשׁ אַחֲרִית, וְאַחַר כָּךְ הַקִּוּוּי לְשֶׁל מַעְלָה
the explanation is that every spiritual level has its culmination (acharit), following which comes yearning (tikvah) to ascend to the next higher realm;
וּמִי שֶׁאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ, לְעוֹלָם עוֹמֵד בְּמַדְרֵגָתוֹ, וְאֵין לוֹ אַחֲרִית וּמִמֵּילָא שֶׁאֵין לוֹ תִקְוָה
and one whom the Holy One, Blessed be He, does not assist remains stagnant in his level, possessing no culmination and consequently having no forward hope.
שָׁם: "יְהִי רָצוֹן" וְכוּלֵי
There: the personal prayers of the Sages after the Amidah:
הִתְבּוֹנֵן בְּאֵלֶּה הַתְּפִלּוֹת: דְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בִּקְּשׁוּ כָּל אֶחָד שֶׁבַע בַּקָּשׁוֹת
Contemplate these supplications carefully: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan each formulated exactly seven requests;
וְרַבִּי זֵירָא וְרַבִּי חִיָּיא כָּל אֶחָד רַק שָׁלֹשׁ
while Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Chiya each formulated only three;
וְרַב וְרַבִּי כָּל אֶחָד עֲשָׂרָה [רַק שֶׁל רַב הֵם תּוֹסֶפֶת טוֹבָה [וְחַיִּים אֲרֻכִּים אֵינוֹ מֵחֶשְׁבּוֹן], וְשֶׁל רַבִּי — הַצָּלָה מֵרָע]

and Rav and Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi] each petitioned for a decade of ten [except that Rav's ten petitions were additions of positive goodness (long life being an overarching preface outside the count), whereas Rabbi's ten were for rescue from evil];
וְהָבֵן אֵיךְ מַקְבִּילִים זֶה לָזֶה וּבִמְכֻוָּן בְּמִסְפָּרִים אֵלּוּ, וְאֵיךְ מְיֻחָדִים לְאוֹתָן הָאוֹמְרִים, וְאֵין כָּאן מָקוֹם לְהַאֲרִיךְ
and understand how they correspond symmetrically in these precise numbers and how they reflect the unique soul-roots of those specific Sages; and this is not the place to elaborate.
שָׁם: "מֵאֲבוֹתֵינוּ"
There: "May we not be ashamed of our ancestors":
פֵּרוּשׁ: הָאָבוֹת הֵם הַלֵּב וָמֹחַ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, וּכְשֶׁלֹּא נֶחֱטָא בְּמַעֲשֶׂה, לֹא נִכָּלֵם בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה
the explanation is that the "Fathers" represent the heart and the brain, as noted above; and when we do not sin in physical action, we will not be humiliated in the inner realm of thought.
[דַּף י״ז עַמּוּד א׳] "בְּקֶרֶן אוֹר"
[Folio 17a]: "In a ray of light and not in a ray of darkness":
פֵּרוּשׁ: "קֶרֶן" — הֶאָרָה, כְּמוֹ קַרְנֵי אוֹר, שֶׁיֵּשׁ הֶאָרָה נִשְׂגָּבָה וּמַחְשֶׁכֶת עֵינָיו מֵרֹב זָהֳרָהּ

The explanation is: "ray" (keren) signifies a flash of illumination, like beams of light, for an illumination can be so overwhelmingly transcendent that it blinds mortal eyes from its sheer brilliance.
וְזֶהוּ "קֶרֶן חֲשֵׁכָה", וְאָז הַלֵּב דָּוֶה שֶׁאֵינוֹ יָכוֹל לְהַשִּׂיג אוֹתוֹ אוֹר, וְהָעַיִן נֶחְשָׁךְ לְהִסְתַּכֵּל אַף לְמַטָּה
And this is a "ray of darkness," where the heart faints because it cannot grasp that blinding light, and the eye is darkened from viewing even lower realities;
וְהַיְנוּ שֶׁלֹּא יָצִיץ לְמַעְלָה מִמַּדְרֵגָתוֹ
meaning that one should not gaze presumptuously beyond his spiritual stature.
שָׁם: "סִפְרָא דְּאִיּוֹב"
There: "When Rabbi Yochanan concluded the Book of Job, he said: The end of man is to die, and the end of cattle is to slaughter":
שֶׁמָּלֵא מִקֻּשְׁיוֹת "צַדִּיק וְרַע לוֹ", אָמַר הָכֵי לְנֶחָמָה
Because Job is saturated with the agonizing dilemma of "the righteous who suffers," Rabbi Yochanan articulated this as deep consolation:
כִּי "שֶׁמֶן טוֹב" הוּא טוּב הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כְּעִנְיַן "מִשְׁמַנֵּי הָאָרֶץ"
for "a good oil" represents the transient pleasures of this world, in the sense of "the fatness of the earth";
וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁסּוֹף אָדָם לָמוּת, אִם כֵּן כָּל הַתַּעֲנוּגִים כְּאֶפֶס נֶחְשָׁבוּ
and since the end of man is to die, all worldly pleasures are reckoned as absolute nullity.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בַּעַל הַשֵּׁם טוֹב, שֶׁאֶצְלוֹ "טוֹב יוֹם הַמָּוֶת מִיּוֹם הִוָּלְדוֹ", הוּא בַּעַל הַתַּעֲנוּג הָאֲמִתִּי
Unlike the master of a "good name" (shem tov), regarding whom "better is the day of death than the day of one's birth," who alone possesses authentic delight;
כִּי אֵין פַּחַד הַמָּוֶת לְנֶגְדּוֹ, שֶׁהוּא הַמַּמְאִיס כָּל הַתַּעֲנוּגֵי הָעוֹלָם, וְכֻלָּם כְּאַיִן מִפַּחְדּוֹ, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֵצֶל זֶה
for the dread of death does not torment him—that very dread which embitters all worldly pleasures, reducing them to nothingness in its shadow—which is not so for the possessor of a good name.
וְזֶהוּ: "אַשְׁרֵי" וְכוּלֵי, כְּהוֹרָאַת מִלַּת "אִשּׁוּר", דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר אַף בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And this is "Praiseworthy (ashrei) is he who grows in Torah," matching the root ishur, signifying happiness even in this world,
כִּדְדָרְשִׁינַן לְעֵיל חֵלֶק א׳ עַל: "אַשְׁרֶיךָ וְטוֹב לָךְ", שֶׁגַּם בְּתַעֲנוּגֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה אַשְׁרָיו כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
as expounded above on "Praiseworthy are you, and it shall be well with you," that even within the physical experiences of this world he is joyful.
וּפֵרוּשׁ "אָדָם וּבְהֵמָה" עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּפֶרֶק קַמָּא דְּחֻלִּין (דַּף ה׳ עַמּוּד ב׳): שֶׁדּוֹמִין וְכוּלֵי
And the phrase "the end of man is death and the end of cattle is slaughter" mirrors what is taught in Chullin (5b): "those who are shrewd in knowledge and conduct themselves humbly like a beast";
וּמִיתָה הַיְנוּ בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם (שַׁבָּת דַּף ק״ח עַמּוּד ב׳), וּשְׁחִיטָה הִיא פְּעֻלַּת הָאָדָם לַהֲנָאָתוֹ
where bodily death is wrought directly by Heaven, while slaughter is an intentional human act for man's consumption,
כִּי רְשָׁעִים הֵם לְצֹרֶךְ הַצַּדִּיקִים, וְנִכָּר מִסּוֹפָן
for the existence of the wicked ultimately serves the spiritual elevation of the righteous, which becomes recognizable at their end;
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה (דַּף י״ז עַמּוּד א׳): "אֵפֶר תַּחַת כַּפּוֹת רַגְלָן [שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים]", כְּדֵי שֶׁיְּהֵא רַךְ לֵילֵךְ
as stated in Rosh Hashanah (17a): the wicked turn to ashes "under the soles of the feet of the righteous," providing a soft path upon which to tread;
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (חֲגִיגָה דַּף ט״ו עַמּוּד א׳): "זָכָה — נוֹטֵל חֶלְקוֹ וְחֵלֶק חֲבֵרוֹ [בְּגַן עֵדֶן]" וְכוּלֵי
and in Chagigah (15a): "If a righteous man merits, he receives his portion and the portion of his wicked counterpart in the Garden of Eden";
וּלְכָךְ נִבְרָא לְצֹרֶךְ הַצַּדִּיק, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא הִתְעַלּוּת גַּם לָרְשָׁעִים עַל יְדֵי שֶׁזֶּה נֶהֱנֶה מִמֶּנּוּ
thus the wicked was created to serve the rectification of the tzaddik, and through this the wicked is elevated as well when the tzaddik derives sacred purpose from him,
וְהַעֲלָאַת נֶפֶשׁ בְּהֵמָה בִּשְׁחִיטָה, שֶׁאָדָם נוֹטֵל חֶלְקָהּ
just as the soul of a beast is elevated through kosher slaughter when man consumes and elevates its sparks.
וְ"הַכֹּל לְמִיתָה" וְכוּלֵי — הַיְנוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And "all are destined for death"—this applies strictly to this physical world;
רַק "אַשְׁרֵי" וְכוּלֵי דְּזוֹכֶה לַסּוֹף, רָצָה לוֹמַר סוֹף הַכֹּל דְּהַיְנוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא, זֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי שֵׁם טוֹב
but "praiseworthy is he who grows in Torah" who merits the ultimate End—the World to Come—which is attained through a "good name."
כְּטַעַם: "וְנָתַתִּי לָהֶם בְּבֵיתִי וּבְחוֹמֹתַי [יָד וָשֵׁם]... שֵׁם טוֹב" וְגוֹמֵר
This matches the verse: "And I will give them in My house and within My walls... a good name," etc.:
פֵּרוּשׁ "בֵּיתִי" הַיְנוּ בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הַשְּׁלִישִׁי שֶׁהוּא לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
where "My house" refers to the Third Holy Temple of the World to Come,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק חֵלֶק (סַנְהֶדְרִין דַּף צ׳ עַמּוּד א׳) דְּ"אֶרֶץ" נִקְרָא עוֹלָם הַבָּא
and as taught at the opening of chapter Chelek (Sanhedrin 90a), that "land" symbolizes the World to Come
[וְזֶה: "מִבָּנִים וּמִבָּנוֹת" — נוֹחֲלֵי הָאָרֶץ, זֶה לוֹקֵחַ מֵהֶם]
[and this is "better than sons and daughters"—the heirs of earthly land, which he absorbs from them],
וּבִשְׂכַר שְׁמִירַת שַׁבָּת שֶׁהִיא מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא (בְּרָכוֹת דַּף נ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳)
and as the reward for keeping the Sabbath, which is a foretaste of the World to Come (Berakhot 56b).
וְזֶהוּ: "שֵׁם עוֹלָם [אֶתֶּן לוֹ] אֲשֶׁר לֹא יִכָּרֵת", כָּאן רָמוּז שֵׁם הַכֶּתֶר דִּבְרִיאָה כַּנּוֹדָע
And this is "an everlasting name which shall not be cut off," alluding to the Supernal Crown of the World of Creation (Keter d'Beriah), as is known;
וְכַנּוֹדָע דְּרֹאשׁ לַשּׁוּעָלִים הוּא זְנַב לָאֲרָיוֹת, שֶׁהִיא סוֹד הָאָרֶץ כַּנּוֹדָע, וְאֵין כָּאן מָקוֹם לְהַאֲרִיךְ
and as is known that the head of the foxes is the tail of the lions, which is the esoteric mystery of the Holy Land; and this is not the place to elaborate further.
